sections.content: Wholesaling real estate is one of the most accessible entry points into the real estate investing world. You don't need a license, a massive bank account, or years of experience to get started. In fact, many investors close their first wholesale deal within 30 to 90 days of learning the basics. If you want a full overview before diving in, check out our [Wholesale Real Estate for Beginners: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesale-real-estate-beginners-guide) — it's a great companion to what we'll cover here. This article breaks down exactly how to wholesale real estate step by step, so you can go from zero to your first check as quickly as possible.
What Is Real Estate Wholesaling?

Wholesaling is the process of finding a deeply discounted property, getting it under contract, and then selling that contract to a cash buyer for a profit. You never actually buy the home. Instead, you act as the middleman — or deal finder — and collect an assignment fee, typically anywhere from $5,000 to $20,000 or more per deal. It's a strategy built on relationships, hustle, and knowing how to evaluate numbers quickly. If you're brand new to real estate, our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) guide is a smart starting point to understand the bigger picture.
Step 1: Learn Your Market Inside and Out

Before you send a single piece of mail or knock on one door, you need to understand your local market. Study neighborhoods. Know the difference between a $120,000 house and a $180,000 house in your target zip code. Research average days on market, median home prices, and which areas attract the most cash buyers. High-activity wholesale markets like [Atlanta, GA](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Houston, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/houston-tx), and [Phoenix, AZ](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) are great places to see what active deal flow looks like and benchmark your own market research.

Pro Tip: Spend two to three weeks driving your target neighborhoods before you start marketing. Note vacant homes, overgrown yards, and properties with deferred maintenance. These are often your best leads.
Step 2: Find Motivated Sellers

Motivated sellers are the backbone of every wholesale deal. These are homeowners who need to sell quickly — often due to divorce, job loss, inherited property, tax liens, or tired landlord syndrome. You're not trying to take advantage of anyone; you're solving a real problem by offering speed and certainty in exchange for a discount on price.
Top Lead Generation Strategies

items: Direct mail: Send postcards to absentee owners, tax-delinquent properties, and pre-foreclosures
Driving for dollars: Physically scout neighborhoods for distressed properties
Cold calling: Pull lists from PropStream or similar tools and dial leads
Bandit signs: Place 'We Buy Houses' signs in high-traffic areas
Facebook and Google ads: Run targeted ads to motivated seller landing pages
Networking: Build relationships with probate attorneys, divorce attorneys, and real estate agents who encounter distressed sellers

sections.content: Most beginners spread themselves too thin by trying every strategy at once. Pick one or two lead sources, work them consistently for 60 to 90 days, and track your results before adding more channels.
Step 3: Analyze the Deal Using the Right Numbers

This is where most beginners make costly mistakes. Before you make an offer, you need to know three numbers: the After Repair Value (ARV), the estimated repair costs, and your Maximum Allowable Offer (MAO). The standard formula is: MAO = (ARV x 70%) minus Repair Costs minus Your Assignment Fee. For example, if a home has an ARV of $200,000 and needs $30,000 in repairs, your MAO would be roughly $110,000 minus your assignment fee. To avoid guesswork, use our free [Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to run your numbers fast and accurately before making any offer.
"The money in wholesaling is made when you buy, not when you sell. If the numbers don't work on paper, they won't work in real life." — Common wisdom among experienced wholesalers
Step 4: Make an Offer and Get the Property Under Contract

Once you've run your numbers and confirmed there's a deal, it's time to make an offer. Your offer should be in writing using a standard purchase and sale agreement that includes an assignment clause. This clause allows you to transfer the contract to another buyer. Make sure your contract includes an inspection contingency period so you have time to find a buyer before committing. If the seller accepts, congratulations — you now have equitable interest in the property. Read your state's specific laws around this, as some states require a real estate license for certain wholesaling activities.
Step 5: Build and Market to Your Cash Buyers List

A deal under contract is worthless if you have no one to sell it to. That's why smart wholesalers start building their cash buyers list before they even find their first deal. Your buyers list is your most valuable asset. For a full breakdown of how to do this from scratch, check out our guide on [How to Build a Cash Buyers List from Scratch](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/build-cash-buyers-list). Once you have a deal locked up, send a detailed email blast to your buyers. Include the address, ARV, repair estimate, asking price, and photos. The right buyer will respond within 24 to 48 hours.
Where to Find Cash Buyers Fast

items: Local real estate investor association (REIA) meetings
Public records — search recent all-cash transactions in your county
Facebook groups for local real estate investors
Hard money lenders who work with active flippers
Other wholesalers who may have buyers looking for inventory

sections.content: Step 6: Choose Your Exit Strategy and Close the Deal

Most wholesalers use one of two exit strategies: assignment of contract or double closing. In an assignment, you simply transfer your contract to the buyer and collect your fee at closing — usually with full transparency on what you're making. In a double close, you actually purchase the property and immediately resell it, which keeps your profit private. Both have pros and cons depending on the deal, your buyer's preferences, and your state's laws. For a detailed comparison, read our article on [Double Close vs Assignment: Which Wholesale Exit Strategy?](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/double-close-vs-assignment) to decide which approach fits your situation best.
Step 7: Avoid the Mistakes That Kill Beginner Deals

Even with the right process, beginners often stumble on avoidable errors. Overestimating ARV, underestimating repairs, or locking up a property with no buyers lined up are among the most common deal-killers. Before you go all in, take time to review the [7 Wholesale Real Estate Mistakes Beginners Make](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/wholesale-real-estate-mistakes) — it could save you thousands of dollars and weeks of frustration on your first few deals.

Pro Tip: Never stop building your pipeline. While you're working to close one deal, keep marketing for the next. Consistency is the difference between one-time wholesalers and investors who do 5 to 10 deals per month.
What to Expect on Your First Deal

Your first wholesale deal will take longer than you think and teach you more than any course ever could. Expect your first assignment fee to fall somewhere between $3,000 and $15,000. You'll make mistakes, have sellers back out, and deal with buyers who ghost you. That's normal. Every deal sharpens your instincts and expands your network. Most successful wholesalers say their second and third deals came far easier than the first — because by then, they had a process, a buyers list, and real confidence behind their offers.
